subject: math
cluster: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical and quantitative variables

items.prompt:
A class of $25$ students was surveyed about whether they walk or ride a bus to school. The two-way frequency table below is complete.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Walk} & \text{Bus} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Boys} & 6 & 7 & 13 \\ \text{Girls} & 5 & 7 & 12 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 11 & 14 & 25 \end{array}$

How many students in the class are girls who ride the bus?

steps: Find the row labeled Girls and the column labeled Bus.
Read the value in the cell where that row and column meet.
The Girls and Bus cell contains $7$.
So $7$ students are girls who ride the bus.

items.prompt:
Using the same table of $25$ students:

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Walk} & \text{Bus} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Boys} & 6 & 7 & 13 \\ \text{Girls} & 5 & 7 & 12 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 11 & 14 & 25 \end{array}$

What is the joint relative frequency of being a boy who walks? Give your answer as a fraction, a decimal, and a percent.

steps: A joint relative frequency is a single cell count divided by the grand total.
The Boys and Walk cell contains $6$ and the grand total is $25$.
Divide: $\frac{6}{25}$.
As a decimal, $\frac{6}{25}=0.24$.
As a percent, $0.24=24\%$.
So the joint relative frequency is $\frac{6}{25}=0.24=24\%$.

items.prompt:
A survey of $50$ people recorded whether they prefer tea or coffee. The complete table is shown.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Tea} & \text{Coffee} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Adults} & 12 & 18 & 30 \\ \text{Teens} & 8 & 12 & 20 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 20 & 30 & 50 \end{array}$

What is the marginal relative frequency of preferring coffee? Express your answer as a percent.

steps: A marginal relative frequency uses a row or column total divided by the grand total.
The Coffee column total is $30$ and the grand total is $50$.
Divide: $\frac{30}{50}$.
As a percent, $0.6=60\%$.
So the marginal relative frequency of preferring coffee is $60\%$.

items.prompt:
Using the same survey of $50$ people:

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Tea} & \text{Coffee} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Adults} & 12 & 18 & 30 \\ \text{Teens} & 8 & 12 & 20 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 20 & 30 & 50 \end{array}$

What is the joint relative frequency of being a teen who prefers tea? Give your answer as a percent.

steps: A joint relative frequency is one cell count divided by the grand total.
The Teens and Tea cell contains $8$ and the grand total is $50$.
Divide: $\frac{8}{50}$.
As a decimal, $\frac{8}{50}=0.16$.
As a percent, $0.16=16\%$.
So the joint relative frequency is $16\%$.

items.prompt:
In a study of $100$ households, each was classified by whether it owns a dog and whether it owns a cat. The complete table is shown.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Owns Cat} & \text{No Cat} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Owns Dog} & 20 & 35 & 55 \\ \text{No Dog} & 15 & 30 & 45 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 35 & 65 & 100 \end{array}$

What is the marginal relative frequency of owning a dog? Express your answer as a percent.

steps: A marginal relative frequency uses a row or column total divided by the grand total.
The Owns Dog row total is $55$ and the grand total is $100$.
Divide: $\frac{55}{100}$.
As a percent, $\frac{55}{100}=55\%$.
So the marginal relative frequency of owning a dog is $55\%$.

items.prompt:
A survey of students recorded whether they own a pet and whether they have a sibling. The complete table is shown.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Has Sibling} & \text{No Sibling} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Owns Pet} & 32 & 18 & 50 \\ \text{No Pet} & 21 & 9 & 30 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 53 & 27 & 80 \end{array}$

Of those students who own a pet, what fraction have a sibling? Give your answer as a fraction and a percent.

steps: The phrase "of those who own a pet" tells you to condition on pet owners, so the denominator is the Owns Pet row total, $50$, not the grand total.
The number of pet owners who have a sibling is the cell value $32$.
Divide by the row total: $\frac{32}{50}$.
As a decimal, $\frac{32}{50}=0.64$.
As a percent, $0.64=64\%$.
So the conditional relative frequency is $\frac{32}{50}=64\%$.

items.prompt: In a survey of $80$ students, $35$ are boys. Of the boys, $20$ play a sport. Among the girls, $30$ play a sport. Complete the two-way frequency table for gender versus playing a sport, including all marginal totals and the grand total. State the number of girls who do NOT play a sport.
items.answer: $15$ girls do not play a sport

steps: There are $80$ students total and $35$ are boys, so the number of girls is $80-35=45$.
Of the $35$ boys, $20$ play a sport, so boys who do not play a sport: $35-20=15$.
Among the $45$ girls, $30$ play a sport, so girls who do not play a sport: $45-30=15$.
Column totals: play a sport $=20+30=50$; do not play $=15+15=30$.

Check: $50+30=80$ matches the grand total. The completed table is $\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Sport} & \text{No Sport} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Boys} & 20 & 15 & 35 \\ \text{Girls} & 30 & 15 & 45 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 50 & 30 & 80 \end{array}$
So $15$ girls do not play a sport.

items.prompt:
A two-way table of $120$ people cross-classifies preference (coffee or tea) by age group (under 30 or 30 and over). The complete table is shown.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Coffee} & \text{Tea} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Under } 30 & 18 & 22 & 40 \\ 30\text{ and over} & 48 & 32 & 80 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 66 & 54 & 120 \end{array}$

Given that a person is under $30$, what is the conditional relative frequency that they prefer coffee? Round to the nearest whole percent.

steps: The condition "given that a person is under 30" means the denominator is the Under 30 row total, $40$.
The number of under-30 people who prefer coffee is the cell value $18$.
Divide by the row total: $\frac{18}{40}$.
As a decimal, $\frac{18}{40}=0.45$.
As a percent, $0.45=45\%$.
So the conditional relative frequency is $45\%$.

items.prompt:
A school surveyed $200$ students about whether they participate in band and whether they participate in a sport. Some entries are missing.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Band} & \text{No Band} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Sport} & 30 & ? & 110 \\ \text{No Sport} & ? & 65 & ? \\ \hline \text{Total} & 55 & ? & 200 \end{array}$

Fill in the missing values, then compute the conditional relative frequency that a student plays a sport, given that the student is in band. Express the answer as a fraction and a percent.

steps: Sport row: the row total is $110$ and the Band cell is $30$, so No Band $=110-30=80$.
Band column: the column total is $55$ and the Sport cell is $30$, so No Sport in Band $=55-30=25$.
No Sport row total: $25+65=90$. Check: $110+90=200$ matches the grand total.
No Band column total: $80+65=145$. Check: $55+145=200$ matches the grand total.
Now condition on band: "given that the student is in band" uses the Band column total $55$ as the denominator.
Students in band who play a sport: the cell value $30$.
Divide: $\frac{30}{55}=\frac{6}{11}\approx 0.545=54.5\%$, which rounds to $55\%$.
So the conditional relative frequency is $\frac{30}{55}\approx 55\%$.

items.prompt:
Using the survey of $120$ people from item 8:

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Coffee} & \text{Tea} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Under } 30 & 18 & 22 & 40 \\ 30\text{ and over} & 48 & 32 & 80 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 66 & 54 & 120 \end{array}$

A classmate says the marginal relative frequency of preferring tea is $\frac{22}{120}$. Explain the error and give the correct marginal relative frequency of preferring tea as a percent.
items.answer: The classmate used a single cell instead of the Tea column total; the correct marginal relative frequency is $\frac{54}{120}=45\%$

steps: A marginal relative frequency for preferring tea must use the Tea column total, not one cell.
The classmate used $22$, which is only the under-30 tea cell, so $\frac{22}{120}$ is actually the joint relative frequency of being under 30 and preferring tea.
The correct denominator stays $120$ (the grand total), but the numerator must be the full Tea column total: $22+32=54$.
As a percent, $0.45=45\%$.
So the correct marginal relative frequency of preferring tea is $\frac{54}{120}=45\%$.

items.prompt:
A researcher records handedness and gender for $200$ people.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Left-handed} & \text{Right-handed} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Male} & 12 & 88 & 100 \\ \text{Female} & 9 & 91 & 100 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 21 & 179 & 200 \end{array}$

Compute the conditional relative frequency of being left-handed given male, and the conditional relative frequency of being left-handed given female. Compare them and state whether there appears to be an association between gender and handedness. Justify numerically.
items.answer: Given male $\frac{12}{100}=12\%$; given female $\frac{9}{100}=9\%$. The conditionals differ ($12\%$ vs. $9\%$), so there appears to be a slight association, with males somewhat more likely to be left-handed.

steps: Condition on male: denominator is the Male row total $100$, numerator is the left-handed male cell $12$, giving $\frac{12}{100}=0.12=12\%$.
Condition on female: denominator is the Female row total $100$, numerator is the left-handed female cell $9$, giving $\frac{9}{100}=0.09=9\%$.
Compare the two conditional relative frequencies: $12\%$ versus $9\%$.
Because the conditional relative frequency of being left-handed depends on gender (it is higher for males), the two variables appear to be associated.

Justification: if there were no association, the conditional percents would be (about) equal; here they differ by $3$ percentage points, so a slight association exists, with males more likely to be left-handed.

items.prompt:
A survey asked $250$ commuters whether they bike to work and whether they live within $2$ miles of work. The complete table is shown.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Bikes} & \text{Does Not Bike} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Within } 2\text{ mi} & 60 & 40 & 100 \\ \text{Over } 2\text{ mi} & 30 & 120 & 150 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 90 & 160 & 250 \end{array}$

Compute the conditional relative frequency of biking among those within $2$ miles and among those over $2$ miles. Compare them and decide whether distance and biking are associated. Justify your conclusion in context.
items.answer: Within $2$ mi: $\frac{60}{100}=60\%$; over $2$ mi: $\frac{30}{150}=20\%$. The conditionals differ greatly ($60\%$ vs. $20\%$), so distance and biking are associated: commuters who live closer are much more likely to bike.

steps: Condition on living within $2$ miles: denominator is the Within 2 mi row total $100$, numerator is the bikers cell $60$, giving $\frac{60}{100}=60\%$.
Condition on living over $2$ miles: denominator is the Over 2 mi row total $150$, numerator is the bikers cell $30$, giving $\frac{30}{150}=0.2=20\%$.
Compare: $60\%$ versus $20\%$.
The conditional relative frequency of biking changes a lot depending on distance, so the two variables are associated.
In context: people who live within $2$ miles of work are three times as likely to bike ($60\%$ vs. $20\%$), suggesting that shorter distance encourages biking.

items.prompt:
A study of $300$ students records whether they study with a group and whether they passed a final exam.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Passed} & \text{Did Not Pass} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Group Study} & 144 & 36 & 180 \\ \text{Studied Alone} & 72 & 48 & 120 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 216 & 84 & 300 \end{array}$

A student claims that because $216$ of $300$ students passed overall ($72\%$), group study has no effect. Use conditional relative frequencies to evaluate this claim. State whether an association exists and explain why the overall marginal percent alone cannot answer the question.
items.answer: Pass rate given group study $\frac{144}{180}=80\%$; given studied alone $\frac{72}{120}=60\%$. These differ ($80\%$ vs. $60\%$), so study method and passing are associated. The overall $72\%$ is a marginal percent and cannot reveal this because it averages the two groups together.

steps: Condition on group study: denominator is the Group Study row total $180$, numerator is the passed cell $144$, giving $\frac{144}{180}=0.8=80\%$.
Condition on studying alone: denominator is the Studied Alone row total $120$, numerator is the passed cell $72$, giving $\frac{72}{120}=0.6=60\%$.
Compare the conditionals: $80\%$ versus $60\%$.
Since the pass rate depends on the study method, study method and passing are associated.
The student's $72\%$ is the marginal relative frequency of passing ($\frac{216}{300}$), which blends both groups into one number and hides the difference between them.
Only comparing conditional relative frequencies across the two study methods can reveal the association, so the claim that group study has no effect is not supported.

items.prompt:
A town surveyed residents about owning an electric car and recycling regularly. Some entries are missing.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Recycles} & \text{Does Not Recycle} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Electric Car} & ? & 10 & 60 \\ \text{No Electric Car} & 90 & ? & 140 \\ \hline \text{Total} & ? & ? & 200 \end{array}$

Complete the table. Then compute the conditional relative frequency of recycling for electric-car owners and for non-owners, compare them, and state whether owning an electric car is associated with recycling. Justify numerically.
items.answer: Electric-car owners: $\frac{50}{60}\approx 83\%$; non-owners: $\frac{90}{140}\approx 64\%$. The conditionals differ ($83\%$ vs. $64\%$), so owning an electric car is associated with recycling: owners recycle at a noticeably higher rate.

steps: Electric Car row: total $60$ with $10$ not recycling, so Recycles $=60-10=50$.
No Electric Car row: total $140$ with $90$ recycling, so Does Not Recycle $=140-90=50$.
Recycles column total: $50+90=140$. Does Not Recycle column total: $10+50=60$. Check: $140+60=200$ matches the grand total.
Condition on electric-car owners: denominator is the Electric Car row total $60$, numerator $50$, giving $\frac{50}{60}=\frac{5}{6}\approx 0.833=83\%$.
Condition on non-owners: denominator is the No Electric Car row total $140$, numerator $90$, giving $\frac{90}{140}=\frac{9}{14}\approx 0.643=64\%$.
Compare: $83\%$ versus $64\%$. The recycling rate is higher among electric-car owners, so the two variables are associated, with owners more likely to recycle.

items.prompt:
A gym studies $240$ members, classifying each by membership type (basic or premium) and whether they attended at least $10$ classes last month. The complete table is shown.

$\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Attended }10+ & \text{Attended Fewer} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Basic} & 36 & 84 & 120 \\ \text{Premium} & 60 & 60 & 120 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 96 & 144 & 240 \end{array}$

The manager argues that since both membership types have the same total of $120$ members, type cannot affect attendance. Compute the conditional relative frequency of attending $10+$ classes for each membership type, compare them, and explain why equal marginal totals do not imply no association. State your conclusion in context.
items.answer: Basic: $\frac{36}{120}=30\%$; Premium: $\frac{60}{120}=50\%$. The conditionals differ ($30\%$ vs. $50\%$), so membership type and attendance are associated. Equal marginal totals only describe group sizes, not attendance rates, so they cannot rule out association.

steps: Condition on basic members: denominator is the Basic row total $120$, numerator is the attended-10+ cell $36$, giving $\frac{36}{120}=0.3=30\%$.
Condition on premium members: denominator is the Premium row total $120$, numerator is the attended-10+ cell $60$, giving $\frac{60}{120}=0.5=50\%$.
Compare the conditional relative frequencies: $30\%$ versus $50\%$.
Because the rate of attending $10+$ classes depends on membership type, the two variables are associated.
The equal marginal totals ($120$ and $120$) only say the two groups are the same size; they say nothing about the attendance rate within each group, so they cannot show whether an association exists.
In context: premium members attend $10+$ classes at a higher rate ($50\%$ vs. $30\%$), so the manager's argument is incorrect and membership type is associated with attendance.
